explain.say: Have you ever taken a photo that felt a bit boring, even though the view was amazing? Often a tiny move fixes it. Photographers use a trick called the rule of thirds. Look at the first step: turn on the grid in your phone camera, two lines across and two lines down.

explain.say: Now the horizon. Instead of cutting the picture in half, put the horizon on a grid line. Look at the bar: land fills two thirds, sky fills one third. Which would you give more space to on a cloudy, dramatic day?

Look at the board to compare. A subject in the middle can feel stiff and still, like a passport photo. On a third line, the photo feels lively and leaves space to show where the subject is. Which would you choose for a photo of a runner?

faq.q: What is the rule of thirds?
faq.a: The rule of thirds divides a picture into nine equal boxes with two lines across and two down. Placing the subject on the lines or where they cross often makes a photo more balanced and interesting.
asks: How does the rule of thirds work?

faq.q: Why not put the subject in the middle?
faq.a: A centred subject can look stiff and leaves no room to show where it is. Off-centre placement creates movement and balance. But centring still works well for symmetrical scenes.
asks: Is it bad to centre a photo?
When should I centre the subject?

faq.q: Where should I put the horizon in a photo?
faq.a: Usually on the top or bottom grid line: give two thirds to the sky if it is dramatic, or two thirds to the land or sea if that is more interesting.
asks: Should the horizon be in the middle?
How do I photograph a sunset?

faq.a: Looking room, or lead room, is empty space left in front of where a person is looking or a thing is moving, so the photo feels natural rather than cramped.
asks: What is lead room in photography?
Where should space go in a portrait?

faq.q: Is the rule of thirds a strict rule?
faq.a: No, it is a helpful guide. Great photos sometimes break it on purpose, for example with perfect symmetry or a subject right in the centre.
asks: Can I break the rule of thirds?
Do professional photographers always use it?

facts: The term rule of thirds was coined by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery.
A rule of thirds grid divides an image into nine equal parts with four crossing points.

quiz.say: Using the rule of thirds, where is the best place to put your subject?
quiz.show: The rule of thirds puts the subject…

options.show: Right at the edge of the frame
options.say: Right at the edge of the frame

quiz.why: The crossing points draw the eye and balance the picture.

wrong.1: The centre is what the rule helps you move away from.
wrong.2: Right at the edge can cut the subject off.

quiz.say: You photograph a beach with a boring grey sky. Where should the horizon go?
quiz.why: A high horizon gives two thirds of the photo to the more interesting beach and sea.

wrong.1: The middle splits the photo into two equal, less interesting halves.
wrong.2: A low horizon would give most of the picture to the dull sky.
